mary-magdalene-51020.label_copy: The Dutch artist Hendrick Goltzius carved, inked, and printed woodblocks in different colors to create the illusion of dramatic light and shadow, or chiaroscuro, in this depiction of Mary Magdalene. According to the New Testament of the Bible, she was a follower of Jesus Christ and the first person to witness his resurrection. Over time, her story has taken on those of other early Christian women, some of whom were also named Mary or who appear in the Gospels as anonymous figures. one-hundred-christian-emblems-emblematum.label_copy: This is an emblem book, a literary genre popular in Europe during the 1500s and 1600s. These volumes featured texts and illustrations designed to communicate moral lessons and stir the reader’s imagination. This example stands out for at least three reasons. It is the first and only written by a woman, Georgette de Montenay, and the first to include intaglio engravings rather than woodcut illustrations. It is also the first Protestant example of the genre, produced during a prolonged civil war between Catholics and Protestants in France. penitent-magdalene-glory-821902.label_copy: This manuscript fragment shows Mary Magdalene lifted up by angels during her daily prayers. Some religious accounts claim she was a sex worker before she met Jesus, and that after his death she chose to live in contemplative solitude. Images from the medieval period onward often depict her in the wilderness, her hair grown long enough to cover her naked body. Mary Magdalene has come to represent courage, inclusivity, feminine leadership, and the fullness of human experience. Her spiritual devotion may have been especially inspiring to female patrons commissioning a prayerbook, perhaps this work’s original context. river-landscape-mercury-abducting-psyche.label_copy: Two artists sit high above the banks of a bustling river, sketching the landscape that unfolds before them. Only on second look do we notice the two figures flying through the sky. Though we might suppose the main subject to be the landscape, the figures (and the Latin text below them) allude to Roman mythology. Unlike the heroic love stories told in the paintings to the right and left of this print, this tale can be seen as a loss of consent through violence and deception. Mercury carries Psyche away to Cupid, who had previously held her prisoner in his palace. Ordinary life goes on below, revealing society’s indifference. st-margaret-and-dragon-821901.label_copy: The subject matter and size of this illuminated miniature suggest that it was removed from a small prayer book or a book narrating the lives of the saints. The painting depicts St. Margaret in prayer, standing on a dragon; the saint’s body type and high forehead and the carefully drawn parallel hatching on the faces and robes point to the origin of the illumination in the southern Netherlands, perhaps Flanders. According to legend, St. Margaret was swallowed whole by a dragon but broke free from its womb unscathed. The resonance of this story meant that the saint was often the focus of prayer during pregnancy, her painted or printed image sometimes worn on an amulet or a clutched in the hand during childbirth.
